utpfs7:262: The most troublesome problem with the collision model is information asymmetry: independent researchers have no telemetry, no customer logs, no threat intelligence feeds, so they cannot determine whether the bug they reported is already being exploited in the wild. The author's pragmatic strategy is to "assume the worst" — default to assuming you are not the sole finder, submit the report as quickly as possible and push to shrink the disclosure window, and if the vendor stalls, throw responsibility back on the vendor. At the same time, Linus's criticism of drive-by reports reveals another survival strategy: read the docs, write the patch, add real value on top of AI output. A patch-attached report not only gets fixed faster, it also accumulates "trust capital" — the next time that email lands in the vendor's inbox, it gets prioritized. Essentially, this shifts a researcher's competitiveness from "discovery speed" to "delivery quality."
